content.title: Review
content.review:
The paper proposes to use a gated layer as the classifier (on MNIST images or on top of ResNet backbones) to address task-incremental learning. The gating can theoretically reduce gradient update to the weights, thus reducing forgetting. And its forward pass resembles a dynamic system's time step update, and a dynamic system can have equilibrium points, thus helping with forgetting. The method performs better or comparably when used with existing methods compared to just using the existing methods alone.

Pros:
- The proposed method is easy to implement and easy to understand.
- The analogy with dynamic systems is interesting.
- The method outperforms MLP baseline on most of the datasets and method pairs.

Cons:
- The theory (dynamic system analogy) disconnects with the practice.
  1. The dynamic system assumes the vector progresses through time $t\to\infty$ with infinitesimal $\xi$, and only then we can have sink points for the vector. But in the analogy, equation (7), $\xi$ becomes $T \in [0,1]$ which means really large time steps in the progress, and the time step is different for each dimension of the vector. 
  2. There is no guarantee that the vector field has a sink point that is finite, especially considering the $\mathcal H$ in equation (5) being linear. 
  3. The design of the network (the HCN layer forward passes only once) also means only *one* time step is taken, so there is no reason for the feature vector to converge into a sink position.
  4. It would actually be a problem if the vectors do converge to different sink points for different tasks, because all input from that task will converge to the same representation, making it impossible for a classifier to distinguish classes within the task.
  5. Finally, a vector field may not protect against catastrophic forgetting, because the field is dependent on $W_L$, which can change for e.g. GEM or in the permuted MNIST experiments.
- The novelty is somewhat limited, since it heavily draws on GRUs from RNN LSTMs. And the method is relatively disjoint from the task of incremental learning. It sounds more like a network design improvement beneficial to regular tasks than dealing with catastrophic forgetting.
- Occasional underwhelming performance. 
The method doesn't statistically significantly outperform MLP in half of CIFAR and CUB experiments. (permuted MNIST are not as reliable for incremental learning as per [https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.08101]) It performs better on CUB, but CUB only has 6000 images and only half is used for incremental learning and split among 10 tasks -- it's too small that we get e.g. $44.16\pm 33.26$ ACC.
- Experiment issues.
  1. Figure 3 does not consider the extra network weights in Q used in the gating functions. It is not a fair comparison to compare gradient magnitude on one set of weights vs that on two sets.
  2. Figures in Section 4.3-4.6 should use BWT instead of just the first task.
  3. Comparison to large-MLP should be there for Section 4.5 -- although in 4.4 they're not much better than MLP, but they are still better than the rest. The results in 4.5 are so close that a comparison would be preferred.
  4. Computation of statistical significance is hard to understand. For example, in Section 4.5 CUB (Table 2), we have  $44.16\pm 33.26$ vs  $38.91\pm 29.54$ is $p<0.01$, but it's unknown if 33.26 is $\sigma$ or $3\sigma$. Also why GEM and EWC's results are so similar but one is $p<0.01$ while the other is $p>0.5$ is hard to decipher.

Summary:

Despite the interesting analogy to dynamic systems, it seems to fail due to too many differences. Also considering the experiment making no difference for many dataset-method pairs and the limited novelty, this paper needs more work to be considered.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

display_title: HCN - An highway network approach to prevent catastrophic forgetting for task fine-tuning

content.title: HCN - An highway network approach to prevent catastrophic forgetting for task fine-tuning
content.review:
HCN networks are introduced and evaluated for three datasets and several continual learning techniques and demonstrate that HCN networks can handle sequential continual learning better and that gradients are lower than the alternatives. The authors clearly describe the experimental setup and the evaluation metrics used for the experiments.

The paper's main contributions seem to be in the additional experimentations performed rather than novel methods to avoid catastrophic forgetting. They do not discuss the differences between traditional MLPs with highway connections and HCNs in-depth, but the differences seem to be subtle. Interesting to hear that continual learning techniques work the best when applied to the final layers, but there is little reasoning about why that is. The variance in reported results is relatively high, thus not demonstrating a significant improvement compared to alternatives.

The paper would benefit from a more detailed description of the novelty in HCNs, especially compared to traditional highway connections. Otherwise, they describe the experimental setup well, but the results are not convincing and could also benefit from additional reasoning about why, e.g., the main benefits arise in the final layers.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

display_title: An empirical comparison of MLPs vs Highway networks with an emphasis on continual learning, but not a continual learning paper per se.

content.title: An empirical comparison of MLPs vs Highway networks with an emphasis on continual learning, but not a continual learning paper per se.
content.review:
The paper proposes to "look inwards" and analyse neural network mechanisms to propose architectures that secure learnt knowledge. Central to the catastrophic forgetting is finding the right balance in stability vs plasticity. The paper conceptualises stability for continual learning by viewing neural networks as dynamical systems. The paper focuses on Highway-Connection Classifier Nets (HCNs) and starts by viewing their forward pass process through the different layers as a discrete step dynamical system. They argue that the dynamical system view is a good match for the plasticity and stability trade-off, where multiple equilibria/sinks would allow to represent representations that are appropriate for different tasks. Thus as the data of the different tasks pass through the HCN/dynamical system would end up in different attractors; arguing along the way that such different attractors address plasticity. This is relatively straightforward as the task id is provided together with the training instance. 

Following that discussion the paper discusses how HCNs can prevent over modification of the network parameters through their gating mechanisms, making them thus more resistant to forgetting. The paper proceeds by exploring how vanilla MLPs and HCNs fair in continual learning and then how they do fair when they are coupled with a number of continual learning techiques, the results show that HCNs outperform the MLP variants. 

I do not see in the paper any really new continual learning technique. What I rather see is a relative empirical comparison of the merits of HCNs agains MLPs with the an emphasis on a continual learning setting. I see a strong disconnect between the section that provides a dynamical system perspective to HCNs and the subsequent discussion of how the updates happen in the setting of HCNs. I would have expected the paper to build further on the dynamical system perspective, and provide theoritical or empirical results that support this view. As the paper is now the dynamical system perspective, section 3.1, is almost irrelevant to the rest of the paper. 

At the end the focus of the paper is on how updates happen in HCNs and how that might be beneficial to continual learning. However, as I said above the message that I take from the paper is more of the form :MLPs are better than HCNs.  Going a bit more into details of that part of the paper. Gated units of HCNs can potentially limit the parameter updates since there the weight gradient is given by the standard weigth gradient multiplied by the gate value \in [0,1]. However the scale of the update depends on the gate value, and we cannot really do any clear statement on that, since we do not know how it changes as a function of the instances and as a function of the tasks. Section 3.3 tries to sed some light on the behavior of the gradient updates in HCNs compared to the standard MLPs and ResNets. The paper tracks the evolution of the loss and the gradient norm within a single task and between two tasks, figure 3. The paper claims that the HCNs protect more than ResNet and MLP from catastrophic forgetting becaus the magnitude of the updates is smaller. I am not sure I would interpret in the same way figure 3.b. What I see there is that HCNs have consistently a lower update size compared to the other methods event within the limits of a given task. Under that light the smaller update size when the task changes seems to be less important. What would be more relevant here is to quantify the between task change relative to the average within task gradient change; there I have the feeling that the relative update sizes between tasks of HCNs and MLP and ResNet would be comparable. Moreover, as I said above the scale of the gradient is a function of T_L_\gamma which itself is a function of the data and I am not sure I see something in the optimization problem that limits its size, of course the figure 3 shows that something like might happen, but here we just look at a couple of tasks, and I am not sure we can safely draw conclusions about HCNs having a consistently lower update size than the methods against which it is compared.  

Detail: The statement within the text that the "gradients shown were the mean absolute values of W_L_\gamma of Equations.." is misleading; I guess what is shown is the same quantity but for the gradient and not the set of weights. In addition I guess that these values are actually the ?averaged? values over all parameters and layers.

As a side note, in the setting of continual learning it might be more interesting to see what are the dynamics of the weight updates and how the vector field of the parametr updates looks like and how it is structured by the presence of the different tasks.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

display_title: Potentially an interesting idea but not clearly motivated and mixed experimental results

content.title: Potentially an interesting idea but not clearly motivated and mixed experimental results
content.review:
This paper proposes to use highway connections (an existing method originally devised for improving gradient flow in deep networks) as a means for mitigating catastrophic forgetting for continual learning. Experiments are run in a number of sequential task and incremental class settings, comparing the performance of HCNs to MLPs and Resnets, both in a naive SGD training setting and in combination with a number of existing continual learning methods. Overall, the empirical results demonstrate that HCNs can mitigate forgetting to some extent in the naive SGD setting where it is compared to MLPs with a similar number of parameters, but the remaining experiments compared to MLPs with a smaller number of parameters than the HCN, so it was hard to draw conclusions from the results. The message communicated for why HCNs might improve continual learning is confusing; the motivating hypothesis is that HCNs approximate a dynamical system that can support multiple attractor states to accommodate sequential learning of multiple skills, and later it is hypothesised that the gating mechanism in HCNs is what gives it an advantage. No theoretical or experimental evidence is provided for the first hypothesis, some indirect evidence is given for the second (by showing that the gradient magnitudes are smaller for HCNs than MLPs and Resnets), but it’s not clear how the two relate. 
The idea that HCNs could help to mitigate catastrophic forgetting is an interesting one, and is possibly corroborated by previous successes of using gating mechanisms for continual learning [1,2], but the experimental validation is not entirely convincing and there is not a clear enough intuition or theoretical motivation to compensate for this. For this reason, I cannot recommend it for acceptance in its current form. The paper could be improved by ensuring that the MLPs in all experiments have the same number of parameters as the HCNs, and by providing experiments to test the dynamical systems hypothesis for HCNs.

Positives
- It is an interesting idea to test HCNs in a continual learning setting that may provide some additional evidence for the beneficial use of gating mechanisms for mitigating forgetting.
- HCNs are shown to marginally outperform MLPs and residual networks in a sequential task setting when trained with SGD.
- The use of HCNs is orthogonal to many other standard continual learning techniques and can be combined with them as shown in the experiments with several different existing methods.

Concerns
- It is not clear why large MLPs, with the same number of parameters as the HCN networks, were not used in all experiments. The justification for not doing so seems to be that in the setup where MLPs, large MLPs and HCNs are compared without other continual learning methods, the large MLPs do not outperform the smaller MLPs in terms of forgetting. But the extra parameters could plausibly make a difference to forgetting when combined with other continual learning methods such as EWC, so it’s not clear that comparing EWC+HCN to EWC+MLP is a fair comparison, for example. This makes many of the results in Table 2, which show that HCN mitigates forgetting when combined with other continual learning methods, difficult to take at face value.
The results in Table 2 comparing HCNs and MLPs when combined with other continual learning methods are mixed in terms of the significance of the gains induced by HCNs.
- The motivation for why HCNs can help with continual learning in the paper comes from taking a dynamical systems perspective of HCNs, but the intuition is not clearly explained, nor is the hypothesis tested by the experiments conducted. The paper claims that, since the evolution of neural activity in an HCN can be thought of as time-discretised updates of a continuous dynamical system, it therefore defines a vector field which may have attractor states. The paper hypothesises that the “existence of a common vector field enables the classifier network to possess one contiguous solution space for solving all sequential tasks; and this creates a firm structure that is robust to parametric modifications during continual network updates”. Furthermore, it is claimed that multiple attractors can be learnt, each corresponding to a different skill, allowing many tasks to be learnt sequentially. The reasoning here is not clear - why will the existence of a common vector field yield a structure that is robust to parametric modifications and why will an attractor be learnt for each task in an HCN in the context of sequential learning? The experiments do not address this hypothesis either.
- Later in the paper, in Section 3.3 and in the Related work section, it is hypothesised that the gating mechanism of HCN might play a role in limiting parameter updates and preventing forgetting. The use of gating for continual learning is an interesting one that has been explored previously for continual learning [1,2] (perhaps these papers should be cited), but it is not clear how this fits in with the vector field theory. Some indirect evidence is provided for this hypothesis, as experiments are run in the paper showing that the gradient magnitudes are smaller when using HCN compared to MLPs and Resnets, potentially due to the gating mechanism.
- Shallowest layer results. In Section 4.7, it is shown that freezing the shallowest layer of the HCN after training on the first task gives better results than continuing to train it for all tasks, but is this something that is unique to HCN or is it also the case for MLPs? Results are not shown for MLPs whose shallowest layer is frozen after the first task.
- The abstract is misleading in presenting Highway networks as a new method when it is actually an existing one being tested in a different setting (as stated later in the paper). 
- Code not included.

[1] Beaulieu, Shawn, et al. "Learning to continually learn." arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.09571 (2020).
[2] Masse, Nicolas Y., Gregory D. Grant, and David J. Freedman. "Alleviating catastrophic forgetting using context-dependent gating and synaptic stabilization." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115.44 (2018): E10467-E10475.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct
